extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (patent agents and attorneys), USPTO enrollment & discipline stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements for establishing and certifying micro entity status before the USPTO, the practitioner's duties when presenting such certifications (37 C.F.R. § 11.18), how to count prior applications, and the civil/criminal/disciplinary consequences of false certifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity qualification elements (37 C.F.R. § 1.29 / MPEP § 509.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to qualify as a micro entity, patent applicants must certify that: (1) the applicant qualifies as a small entity as defined in § 1.27; (2) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has been named as the inventor or a joint inventor on more than four previously filed patent applications; (3) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor, in the calendar year preceding the calendar year in which the applicable fee is being paid, had a gross income ... exceeding three times the median household income for that preceding calendar year; and (4) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has assigned, granted, or conveyed, nor is under an obligation by contract or law to assign, grant, or convey, a license or other ownership interest in the application concerned to an entity that ... had a gross income ... exceeding three times the median household income for that preceding calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See generally 37 C.F.R. § 1.29; MPEP § 509.04. The page emphasizes applicants must make these specific factual certifications in writing to claim micro entity fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as 'previously filed patent applications' for the four-application limit
rubrics_metrics.description: "For purposes of establishing micro entity status under the 'gross income' basis, the application filing limit includes: (i) previously filed U.S. nonprovisional applications (e.g., utility, design, plant, continuation, and divisional applications), (ii) previously filed U.S. reissue applications, and (iii) previously filed U.S. national stage applications under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 509.04(a) ('B. Application Filing Limit'). All such applications naming the inventor or a joint inventor are counted toward the application filing limit, whether filed before, on, or after March 19, 2013, and whether pending, patented, or abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications excluded from the four-application count
rubrics_metrics.description: "The application filing limit does not include: (i) foreign applications; (ii) international (PCT) applications for which the basic U.S. national stage filing fee was not paid; and (iii) provisional applications."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, where an applicant/inventor assigned, or is under contractual/law obligation to assign, all ownership rights in the application as the result of previous employment, that person is not considered to be named on the prior filed application for purposes of determining micro entity status. See 37 C.F.R. 1.29(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of the filing-limit on available micro-entity discounted filings
rubrics_metrics.description: "Because the four-application limit is a limit on previously filed U.S. nonprovisional applications, reissue applications, and national stage applications, the maximum number of applications in which fees can be paid at the micro entity discount rate can vary from 0 to 5 for any given inventor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains practical variability in how many applications may nevertheless receive micro-entity fee treatment depending on counting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and form of micro entity certification (written, before or at first micro fee payment)
rubrics_metrics.description: "35 U.S.C. 123 requires a certification as a condition for an applicant to be considered a micro entity. The certification must be in writing and must be filed prior to or at the time a fee is first paid in the micro entity amount in an application or patent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 509.04; also: 'A fee may be paid in the micro entity amount only if it is submitted with, or subsequent to, the submission of a certification of entitlement to micro entity status.' See 37 C.F.R. § 1.29(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent establishment of micro entity status is fraud on the Office (37 C.F.R. § 1.29(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Any attempt to fraudulently establish status or pay fees as a micro entity shall be considered as a fraud practiced or attempted on the Office. Improperly, and with intent to deceive, establishing status or paying fees as a micro entity shall be considered as a fraud practiced or attempted on the Office."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule treats intentional deceptive attempts to claim micro-entity benefits as fraud on the USPTO and subject to agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory penalties for false assertions or certifications of small and micro entity status (35 U.S.C. §§ 41(j) and 123(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered practitioners are reasonably aware that the USPTO rules include statutory penalties for falsely made assertions or certifications of small and micro entity status. As required by statute, the USPTO assesses a fine of not less than three times the amount an entity failed to appropriately pay the USPTO when the entity is found to have falsely made an assertion or certification of small or micro entity status, unless the entity shows the assertion or certification was made in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of July 8, 2025, the USPTO issues a combined notice of payment deficiency and order to show cause when it preliminarily determines a pending application or patent contains a false assertion that resulted in at least one improperly reduced fee; a subsequent notice provides a final determination and fine amount. See 15 Official Gazette 204 (July 8, 2025). The penalty provisions only apply when discounted fees were paid on or after Dec. 29, 2022.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifications when presenting papers — practitioner's duty of reasonable inquiry (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered practitioners make important certifications via 37 C.F.R. § 11.18 whenever presenting any paper to the USPTO. The practitioner certifies that all statements made of his or her own knowledge are true, and that all statements based on the presenter's information and belief are believed to be true. Further, the practitioner certifies that, to the best of the party's knowledge, information and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances: (i) the paper is not being presented for any improper purpose; (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for change; (iii) factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to after reasonable investigation; and (iv) denials are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on lack of information or belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accordingly, a registered practitioner who presents any paper to the USPTO — including certifications of micro entity status — certifies that he or she has conducted an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances that supports the factual assertions set forth in the paper. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(iii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of violating § 11.18 (criminal and disciplinary exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Violations of § 11.18 may jeopardize the probative value of the filing, and any false or fraudulent statements are subject to criminal penalty under 18 U.S.C. § 1001. Any registered practitioner who violates the provisions of this section may also be subject to disciplinary action."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order reinforces that false certifications can lead both to criminal liability under federal law and to USPTO disciplinary proceedings (OED).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner diligence and conduct prejudicial to the administration of the patent application process (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.103 and 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent's acts and omissions violated the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 (diligence) inter alia by (i) not always conducting a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.18 prior to signing and presenting certifications of micro entity status to the USPTO, and (ii) failing to have in place adequate procedures to ensure that certifications of micro entity status complied with USPTO regulations and, instead, relying on the clients' erroneous representations; and 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) (conduct prejudicial to the administration of the patent application process) for similar failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to conduct reasonable inquiry and to maintain adequate procedures are cited as bases for violation of both diligence and prejudicial-conduct rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected remedial/mitigating practices and enforcement/publication of sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions may include public reprimand; publication of the Final Order in the OED FOIA Reading Room and notice in the Official Gazette consistent with the reprimand language. The Office may use the record of the disciplinary proceeding in future matters involving the same or similar misconduct as an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order notes mitigating considerations (no prior discipline, genuine contrition, acceptance of responsibility, and that Respondent implemented new procedures such as stopping acceptance of foreign clients asserting micro entity status and using searches to verify small entity entitlement). It also details procedural consequences (waiver of appeal rights, parties bear own costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern — overreliance on foreign associates/forms without direct verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Order describes the respondent's practice: relying on translated forms and communications from foreign associates rather than direct communication or independent verification of clients' eligibility, and that such reliance without reasonable inquiry was insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an example of inadequate practice, the respondent 'would not ordinarily communicate directly with his foreign applicant clients but instead would rely on input and communications from the foreign associates.' The Order states it was not reasonable to do so and the practitioner must conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.
